cases.title: Split DNS behaviour differs from tailscale's
cases.body:
**Bug description**

Tailscale allows split DNS configurations common for corporate VPNs:

 * queries for corporate domains go to a resolver on the VPN
 * other queries go to local resolver (because I want to use my pihole)

In tailscale config UI, the following configuration results in exactly the above behaviour:

![splitDNS](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6534306/214037588-dd287251-dcc5-4373-a477-13c65442f9cc.png)

My tailscale client logs show this:

```
dns: Set: {DefaultResolvers:[] Routes:{foocorp.com.:[10.1.0.2]} SearchDomains:[foocorp.com.] Hosts:4}
dns: Resolvercfg: {Routes:{} Hosts:4 LocalDomains:[]}
dns: OScfg: {Nameservers:[10.1.0.2] SearchDomains:[foocorp.com.] MatchDomains:[foocorp.com.] Hosts:[]}
```

and `systemd-resolve` agrees:

```bash
# resolvectl status tailscale0
Link 4 (tailscale0)
    Current Scopes: DNS
         Protocols: -DefaultRoute -LLMNR -mDNS -DNSOverTLS DNSSEC=no/unsupported
Current DNS Server: 10.1.0.2
       DNS Servers: 10.1.0.2
        DNS Domain: foocorp.com
```

**To Reproduce**

Equivalent headscale config would be:

```yaml
dns_config:
  override_local_dns: false
  restricted_nameservers:
    foocorp.com:
      - 10.1.0.2
  magic_dns: false
```
However, headscale explictly ignores `dns_config.restricted_nameservers` unless global nameservers are configured. The closest possible config is:

```yaml
dns_config:
  override_local_dns: true
  nameservers:
    - 1.1.1.1

  restricted_nameservers:
    foocorp.com:
      - 10.1.0.2

  domains: ["foocorp.com"]

  magic_dns: false
```
which tailscale sees as:

```
dns: Set: {DefaultResolvers:[1.1.1.1] Routes:{foocorp.com.:[10.1.0.2]} SearchDomains:[foocorp.com.] Hosts:1}
dns: Resolvercfg: {Routes:{.:[1.1.1.1] foocorp.com.:[10.1.0.2]} Hosts:1 LocalDomains:[]}
dns: OScfg: {Nameservers:[100.100.100.100] SearchDomains:[foocorp.com.] MatchDomains:[] Hosts:[]}
```

and results in this local resolver config:

```bash
# resolvectl status tailscale0
Link 4 (tailscale0)
    Current Scopes: DNS
         Protocols: +DefaultRoute -LLMNR -mDNS -DNSOverTLS DNSSEC=no/unsupported
Current DNS Server: 100.100.100.100
       DNS Servers: 100.100.100.100
        DNS Domain: foocorp.com ~.
```

which uses the embedded tailscale DNS server as the default route and therefore bypasses my pihole.

So headscale's behaviour is different to tailscale's and more limited

**Context info**

- Version of headscale used: 0.19.0-beta1
- Version of tailscale client: 1.34.2
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04.1 LTS
- Kernel version: 5.15.0-56-generic

cases.title: Bug: peers not notified of deletion when 2 nodes in network
cases.body:
**Bug description**

* There are two nodes in a tailnet, A and B
* Node B is deleted
* A MapResponse is generated for node A. Node A no longer has any peers, so len(MapResponse.Peers) == 0
* Tailscale interprets len(MapResponse.Peers) == 0 as no change, meaning it isn't notified of node B being deleted https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/blob/43819309e18ac7d496643fcd86489a2ee0927964/control/controlclient/map.go#L227
* Node B remains on tailnet after being deleted, causing a security vulnerability for deleted nodes

Should be fixed by implementing Peer list deltas (sending PeersDeleted explitcly in #1383)

cases.title: MagicDNS base domain clobbers valid records
cases.body:
The Domain used for MagicDNS' base domain must not match an actual domain, as any valid records within such domain are completely clobbered by MagicDNS and return NXDOMAIN.

In my own testing I use my domain (anstee.dev) as the base, knowing full well that MagicDNS will include the namespace ("nicka101" for my testing) in the produced records , and thus there should be no conflict with actual records visible to upstream DNS.

However checking DNS responses after making these changes reveals the following:

Relevant section of headscale config:
 ```
"dns_config": {
        "nameservers": ["8.8.4.4", "8.8.8.8"],
        "domains": [],
        "magic_dns": true,
        "base_domain": "anstee.dev"
    }
```

DNS query for the base domain against 8.8.8.8:
```
❯ dig @8.8.8.8 anstee.dev

; <<>> DiG 9.16.21 <<>> @8.8.8.8 anstee.dev
; (1 server found)
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 11423
;; flags: qr rd ra ad; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 512
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;anstee.dev.                    IN      A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
anstee.dev.             3600    IN      A       51.195.219.36

;; Query time: 116 msec
;; SERVER: 8.8.8.8#53(8.8.8.8)
;; WHEN: Thu Oct 14 01:13:26 CEST 2021
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 55
```

DNS query for base domain against 100.100.100.100:
```
❯ dig @100.100.100.100 anstee.dev

; <<>> DiG 9.16.21 <<>> @100.100.100.100 anstee.dev
; (1 server found)
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 6569
;; flags: qr aa rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 0, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0

;; QUESTION SECTION:
;anstee.dev.                    IN      A

;; Query time: 0 msec
;; SERVER: 100.100.100.100#53(100.100.100.100)
;; WHEN: Thu Oct 14 01:14:34 CEST 2021
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 28
```

Note that its not just the base domain that gets clobbered, any valid subdomains are also clobbered:
```
~ 
❯ dig @8.8.8.8 +noall +answer anstee.dev
anstee.dev.             2876    IN      A       51.195.219.36

~ 
❯ dig @8.8.8.8 +noall +answer git.anstee.dev
git.anstee.dev.         3600    IN      CNAME   anstee.dev.
anstee.dev.             3600    IN      A       51.195.219.36

~ 
❯ dig @100.100.100.100 +noall +answer git.anstee.dev

~ 
❯ dig @8.8.8.8 +noall +answer ldn1.anstee.dev
ldn1.anstee.dev.        3600    IN      A       51.195.219.36

~ 
❯ dig @100.100.100.100 +noall +answer ldn1.anstee.dev

~ 
❯
```

MagicDNS entries themselves are working as expected however:
```
❯ dig @100.100.100.100 +noall +answer pi4.nicka101.anstee.dev
pi4.nicka101.anstee.dev. 600    IN      A       100.99.123.231
```

last_comments.body: I think this is a valid issue. Need to investigate a bit. I reckon we should only capture $NAMESPACE.$BASE_DOMAIN not the whole base domain.

I would tend to agree with Juan that the expected behavior would be for headscale/tailscale to only capture $NAMESPACE.$BASE_DOMAIN (along with any additional namespaces visible to the current user), rather than clobbering the entire base domain.

I understand that the actual DNS responses are controlled by the tailscale client, which is running the DNS server, however it seems like modification of `generateMagicDNSRootDomains` within dns.go could resolve the issue if it were to actually specify the individual relevant subdomains, instead of the base domain itself like it currently does on [dns.go#40](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/main/dns.go#L40)

Yep, I am working on a patch that fixes that already. Will probably launch
a PR today.

cases.title: [Bug] Different A record for nodes with the same name
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [X] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

While testing https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/issues/1369#issuecomment-2339901185, I noticed the following behavior:

#### Setup
* Node with name `laptop` assigned to user `alice` : 100.64.0.2, fd7a:115c:a1e0::2
* Node with name `laptop` assigned to user `bob`:  100.64.0.3, fd7a:115c:a1e0::3
* Config:
  ```yaml
  dns:
    use_username_in_magic_dns: false
    base_domain: tn.example.com
  ```
* Content of `/etc/resolv.conf` on both nodes:
  ```
  nameserver 100.100.100.100
  search tn.example.com
  ```

#### On alice's node
```bash
alice:~$ tailscale ip
100.64.0.2
fd7a:115c:a1e0::2

alice:~$ dig +short laptop.tn.example.com
100.64.0.3
```

#### On bob's node
```bash
bob:~$ tailscale ip
100.64.0.3
fd7a:115c:a1e0::3

bob:~$ dig +short laptop.tn.example.com
100.64.0.2
```

You get a different IP depending on depending on **where** you ask. Interestingly, Tailscale resolves to the IP of the *other* node.

### Expected Behavior

Not sure which IP address, but I'd expect to always get the same one.

### Steps To Reproduce

* Create two users
* Register a node for each user (using unique names, e.g. `laptop` for user `alice` and `server` for user `bob`)
* Run: `headscale nodes rename -i ID_OF_SERVER_BOB laptop`
* Node list:
```
$ headscale nodes list
ID | Hostname  | Name      | MachineKey | NodeKey | User  | IP addresses                  | Ephemeral | Last seen           | Expiration          | Connected | Expired
4  | laptop    | laptop    | [fLttA]    | [J2GVN] | alice | 100.64.0.2, fd7a:115c:a1e0::2 | false     | 2024-09-10 07:53:41 | 0001-01-01 00:00:00 | online    | no
5  | server    | laptop    | [BxUYW]    | [e4Bjc] | bob   | 100.64.0.3, fd7a:115c:a1e0::3 | false     | 2024-09-10 07:55:01 | 0001-01-01 00:00:00 | online    | no
```

### Environment

### Is this a support request?

I just tried to send a file from my vps (that has the tag `tag:server`) to my macbook (that has no tags assigned). And it worked. Without any intervention, it straightup placed the file in my Downloads folder.
The server-tagged devices are not allowed to talk to my personal devices, but fine, Taildrop ignores ACLs. But as it mentions in the docs, that you `cannot use Taildrop to send files to and from nodes you have tagged.`, I think that this is a bug.

Therefore, it should not be possible to send files from tagged nodes to un-tagged nodes and vice versa.

(It also would be amazing if there could be a flag in the config to disable Taildrop completely, as this is also possible to disable in the Tailscale Admin Console. I will create a separate feature request for that.)

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Access a node that has a tag assigned.
2. Prepare the tailnet ip of a target device without tags.
3. Use `sudo tailscale file cp <yourfile.png> <target-ip>:`
4. If the target is linux, use `sudo tailscale file get` to see, if it arrives. on macOS it should already land in the Downloads folder right away.

last_comments.body: This issue was closed because it has been inactive for 14 days since being marked as stale.

For anyone looking for an automated solution to backup the database: I addressed backup'ing the database the follow way. As headscale is started and stopped via systemd, add an override configuration that copies the database to another file each time the service is stopped. In the example below, the backup's filename contains the file's MD5 checksum to avoid having multiple copies of the same database and the headscale version number in case there are incompatible changes across versions. File properties like modification dates are kept when copying, allowing to identify old copies that one can delete.

1. Create the file `/etc/systemd/system/headscale.service.d/backup-config.conf` as follows:
    ```
    [Service]
    ExecStopPost=/usr/bin/bash -c 'cp --verbose --preserve=all /var/lib/headscale/db.sqlite /var/lib/headscale/"$(headscale version|grep -Po --color=NEVER "(?<=v?)[01](\\.[0-9]+)+"|head -n1)"-"$(md5sum <"/var/lib/headscale/db.sqlite"|cut -f1 -d " ")"-db.sqlite'
    ```
2. Tell systemd to reload the updated configuration: `systemctl daemon-reload`

Just tested with the latest stable version:

$ headscale version
headscale version v0.28.0
commit: 97fa117c48a58bee3941e5e8b4393873501afe14
build time: 2026-02-04T20:26:22Z
built with: go1.25.5 linux/amd64

$ headscale version|grep -Po --color=NEVER 
"(?<=v?)[01](\\.[0-9]+)+"|head -n1
0.28.0


I suspect your problem is more related to `grep`. The version I am using 
GNU grep 3.11, where `grep -P` uses "PCRE2 10.46 2025-08-27"

Removing `(?<=v?)` from regular expression the seems to work as well, 
returning the same version string. Test if that works better for you.

cases.title: [Bug] -u --user argument is inconsistent, --identifier/--name unavailable (sometimes --user takes uint, sometimes string)
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

Works as expected:
```
headscale nodes list -u myusername
```

Fails:
```
headscale preauthkeys list -u myusername
invalid argument "myusername" for "-u, --user" flag: strconv.ParseUint: parsing "myusername": invalid syntax
```

Also fails:
```
headscale users rename -u myusername
Error: unknown shorthand flag: 'u' in -u
```

But at least it accepts:
```
  -i, --identifier int    User identifier (ID) (default -1)
  -n, --name string       Username
```


### Expected Behavior

Most commands require a `-u` / `--user` argument, naturally. Perhaps that should be changed to `-i` / `-n` so we can use either a number or name.

Having to look up the ID number of a user is an extra step when scripting, e.g.

```
# Step 1. Get user ID number
USER_ID=$(headscale users show -n {{ HEADSCALE_USER }} --output json | jq -r '.[0].id')
# Step 2. Get preauth keys so we can expire the old ones.
headscale preauthkeys list -u $USER_ID
```

```
headscale preauthkeys list -u myusername
```
should work just as well as
```
headscale nodes list -u myusername
```

Or, it should work like:
```
headscale users rename -n myusername
```
or
```
headscale users rename -i 1234
```

Perhaps the latter is the "new way" and it's in progress?

### Steps To Reproduce

Try the above commands with a real username.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)
- Headscale version: 0.26.0
- Tailscale version: N/A, this is only related to headscale CLI commands

cases.title: [Bug] Headscale reads extra DNS records from path too early
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

I use the `dns.extra_records_path` configuration option to load DNS records from a JSON file. This file is created by a script that combines multiple files into one. The relevant line is:

```bash
jq --sort-keys --slurp 'unique | flatten' dns.d/*.json > /var/lib/headscale/extra-records.json
```

There are about 150 DNS records written to `/var/lib/headscale/extra-records.json` with each invocation. From time to time Headscale's filewatcher picks up the file while it is being written. Presumably, the output buffer is flushed by `jq` and a partial JSON file is persisted for a short while. This causes errors about broken JSON in Headscale's logs:

```
[snipped]
{\\n    \\\"name\\\": \\\"acgmw.example.com\\\",\\n    \\\"type\\\": \\\"A\\\",\\n    \\\"value\\\": \\\"100.64.0.1\\\"\\n  },\\n  {\\n    \\\"name\\\": \\\"acgmx.example.com\\\",\\n    \\\"type\\\": \\\"A\\\",\\n    \\\"value\\\": \\\"100.64.0.1\\\"\\n  },\\n  {\\n    \\\"name\\\": \\\"acgmy.example.com\\\",\\n    \\\"type\\\": \\\"A\\\",\\n    \\\"v\": 
unexpected end of JSON input"
```

As a workaround, I use `stdbuf` to enlarge the output buffer for `jq`:

```bash
stdbuf -o 1M jq --sort-keys --slurp 'unique | flatten' dns.d/*.json > /var/lib/headscale/extra-records.json
```

Is there a way to configure the filewatcher such that it picks up the file once no other process is writing to it?

### Expected Behavior

Unsure what is the best solution to this, some ideas:

- Read the records in `dns.extra_records_path` once no other process writes to it
- Delay the read a bit (probably just a workaround)

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Setup Headscale 0.26.1 with `dns.extra_records_path`
1. Create some sample JSON files
    - [sample-1000.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22057864/sample-1000.json)
    - [sample-100.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22057863/sample-100.json)
    - [sample-10.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22057865/sample-10.json)
    - [gen-extra-records.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22057866/gen-extra-records.py)
1. Update the JSON file with the DNS records: 
    ```bash
    jq --sort-keys --slurp 'unique | flatten' sample-*.json > .headscale/extra-records.json
    ```
1. Observe the error message in Headscale's log

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Debian 13
- Headscale version: 0.26.1
- Tailscale version: -
```

### Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

cases.title: [Bug] Unable to split access to exit nodes
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

For the purpose of documenting the existence of this problem I decided to raise an issue.

It is currently not possible to limit what users can access which exit nodes. With the most restrictive ACLs everyone is still able to use any exit nodes.

As @kradalby mentioned on discord, tailscale has "solved" this by implementing next-gen ACLs named grants with "via" directive. 
As Kristoffer also mentioned, implementing grants is scheduled for 0.31 which is gonna take a lot of time.

As I believe limiting such an access is quite an important feature, I wonder if we can have some workaround with current gen ACLs implemented as a solution.

### Expected Behavior

expected to be able to limit exit nodes access based on ACLs

### Steps To Reproduce

1. set up restrictive acls for exit nodes
2. observe that anyone can still access any exit node

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: alpine
- Headscale version: 0.27.0
- Tailscale version: 64+
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

none

cases.title: [Bug] "Restrict access to exit nodes per user or group" no longer works

last_comments.body:
Confirming on **headscale v0.28.0** with **tailscale 1.96.5 (macOS) / 1.96.4 (Linux) / latest iOS**.

Reproduction is independent of `dst` syntax — tested all of:

- `dst: ["<user>:*", "autogroup:internet:*"]`
- `dst: ["<user>:*", "0.0.0.0/0:*", "::/0:*"]`
- `dst: ["*:*"]`
- `dst: ["*:*", "autogroup:internet:*"]`

…all produce the same end result: `tailscale status` shows `active; exit node;`, `AllowedIPs` on the client contains `0.0.0.0/0` for the exit-node peer, headscale routes are approved — but **0 data packets** ever reach the exit node (`tcpdump -i any -n 'host <client-tailnet-ip>'` on the exit node confirms). Tunnel itself is healthy: `tailscale ping --tsmp <exit-node>` and ICMP to the exit node's tailnet IP both work.

Two independent exit nodes tested to rule out host-specific issues:

- One Debian 13 node co-located with the headscale server (per [FAQ warning](https://headscale.net/stable/about/faq/#can-i-use-headscale-and-tailscale-on-the-same-machine))
- One pristine Debian 13 VPS with only tailscale installed, IP forwarding, UFW with `DEFAULT_FORWARD_POLICY=ACCEPT` and `default allow routed`, `ts-postrouting` MASQUERADE rule present (counter `0 packets, 0 bytes`)

Same symptom on both. Two clients tested (macOS, iOS) — same symptom on both. So the issue is policy-side, not exit-node-side or client-platform-side.

Daemon log on client during a ping attempt:

```
open-conn-track: timeout opening (TCP <client-ip>:nnnn => 1.1.1.1:443); 
                                                          no associated peer node
```

…until ACL is changed away from `autogroup:internet:*`, after which the same flow logs `rejected due to acl` instead. Either way, packets never leave the client.

`tailscale debug netmap` on the client shows the exit-node peer correctly with `AllowedIPs: ["0.0.0.0/0", "100.64.0.x/32", "::/0", ...]`, but the `PacketFilter` array contains zero rules where the client's own tailnet IP appears as a `Src` — so the wgengine has no allow-rule for client-as-source toward `0.0.0.0/0`, and silently drops.

This matches @SymoHTL's analysis exactly: our `src` is a user identity, our exit nodes are tagged — user-src + tagged-dst → empty effective filter for that flow.

Will try the `src: ["*"]` workaround and report back.

Workaround verified: replacing user/group `src` with `src: ["*"]` immediately makes the exit-node flow work end-to-end (`curl https://api.ipify.org` returns the exit node's public IP, ICMP/TCP to arbitrary internet hosts succeeds).

For anyone hitting this with a structured ACL who wants to keep peer-access restrictions and only open the exit-node path, this minimal-permission variant works:

```hujson
"acls": [
  // existing user/group rules KEEP src: ["user@"] / ["group:..."]
  // and KEEP dst restricted to peers (NOT "*:*", NOT autogroup:internet)
  { "action": "accept", "src": ["user@"],        "dst": ["user@:*"] },
  { "action": "accept", "src": ["group:family"], "dst": ["group:family:*"] },

  // ONE additional rule with src: ["*"] just for internet egress via exit nodes
  { "action": "accept", "src": ["*"], "dst": ["autogroup:internet:*"] }
]
```

The trade-off: `src: ["*"]` here grants every tailnet user the right to use any approved exit node. Peer-to-peer access between users stays restricted by the original rules.

Tested combinations that **do not** work (all produce empty effective filter for the user→internet flow when exit nodes are tagged):

- `src: ["user@"], dst: ["autogroup:internet:*"]`
- `src: ["user@"], dst: ["*:*"]`
- `src: ["user@"], dst: ["*:*", "autogroup:internet:*"]`
- `src: ["group:..."], dst: [...]` (any of the above)

The only `src` value that produces a non-empty filter is `["*"]`. So #3087 isn't strictly limited to "Restrict access to exit nodes per user or group" as the title suggests — it's a more general issue with user/group-scoped src against tagged-dst nodes (which exit nodes typically are).

@SymoHTL @thenebu It'd be great if you could [test  a recent nightly build](https://headscale.net/development/setup/install/main/) and migrate to these instructions: https://headscale.net/development/ref/routes/#restrict-access-to-exit-nodes-per-user-or-group

cases.title: Retained rows in `shared_machines` may cause nodes to be accidentally shared later on.
cases.body:
**Bug description**

<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. Describe the expected bahavior
  and how it is currently different. If you are unsure if it is a bug, consider discussing
  it on our Discord server first. -->

Namespace IDs may get reused after consecutive `destroy` and `create` operations.
Internally, shared nodes are represented as a separate relation that maps a machine ID with a destination namespace ID.
While machines belonging to the namespace are removed upon destroying a namespace, shared machines are left untouched.
When a new namespace is created later on, machines previously shared with the old namespace will be treated as shared with the new namespace without further user action or notice.

<!-- Steps to reproduce the behavior. -->
* Create namespace to hold a test node to be shared: `owner`
* Create initial namespace to share with: `another`
* Share a node from `owner` to `another`
* Destroy `another`.
* Create new namespace `yet-another`
* Observe the previously chosen test node being shared with the namespace `yet-another`.

**Context info**

- Version of headscale used: `0.13.0-beta1`

cases.title: Tracking: Flaky integration and unit tests
cases.body:
Tracking issue for flaky tests identified by systematically analyzing CI results across ~75 merged PRs.

Supersedes #2299 and #2935.

## Flaky Tests

Failure rate is approximate, based on ~40 PRs that ran integration tests.

### Critical (~20-42% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestAutoApproveMultiNetwork` (all subtests) — `integration/route_test.go:2037` — ~42% failure rate. ACL/route auto-approve changes don't propagate within EventuallyWithT timeouts on CI runners.
- [ ] `TestACLTagPropagation` — `integration/acl_test.go:2296` — ~20% failure rate. Tag change propagation too slow for CI. Subtests `multiple-tags-partial-removal` and `remove-tag-revokes-access` are worst offenders.

### High (~7-12% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestACLTagPropagationPortSpecific` — `integration/acl_test.go:2852` — ~12%. Port-specific ACL changes via tags don't propagate in time.
- [ ] `TestACLHostsInNetMapTable` — `integration/acl_test.go:101` — ~7%. ACL propagation timing.
- [ ] `TestPingAllByIPManyUpDown` — `integration/general_test.go:1391` — ~7%. Ping failures during up/down cycling.

### Medium (~5% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestAuthWebFlowAuthenticationPingAll` — `integration/auth_web_flow_test.go:18`
- [ ] `TestOIDCExpiryAfterRestart` — `integration/auth_oidc_test.go:1352`
- [ ] `TestEphemeral2006DeletedTooQuickly` — `integration/general_test.go:213`

### Low (~2% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestNodeOnlineStatus` — `integration/general_test.go:1266`
- [ ] `TestAuthWebFlowLogoutAndReloginSameUser` — `integration/auth_web_flow_test.go:60`
- [ ] `TestTagsUserLoginReauthWithEmptyTagsRemovesAllTags` — `integration/tags_test.go:2827`
- [ ] `TestPingAllByIP` — `integration/general_test.go:28`
- [ ] `TestPingAllByIPPublicDERP` — `integration/general_test.go:90`
- [ ] `TestSSHAutogroupSelf` — `integration/ssh_test.go:546`
- [ ] `TestEphemeralInAlternateTimezone` — `integration/general_test.go:131`
- [ ] `TestSubnetRouteACLFiltering` — `integration/route_test.go:2952`

### Unit tests

- [ ] `TestBatcherScalabilityAllToAll` — `hscontrol/mapper/batcher_test.go:580` — Panic: send on closed channel. Race condition in LockFreeBatcher shutdown.
- [ ] `TestAuthenticationFlows` — `hscontrol/auth_test.go:38` — Intermittent 401 from registration cache expiration. (#2935)
- [ ] `TestOIDC024UserCreation` — `integration/auth_oidc_test.go:238` — Non-deterministic DB row ordering. (#2299)

## Common root causes

1. **ACL/tag propagation timing** — Most flakes. EventuallyWithT timeouts too short for CI runners.
2. **Network connectivity races** — Ping timeouts under CI load.
3. **Client startup timeouts** — Tailscale clients don't reach Running state within 2min on slow CI.
4. **Go race conditions** — Actual code bugs (LockFreeBatcher, registration cache).

last_comments.body:
## Update: PR #3145 (integration test infrastructure standardization)

#3145 addresses several infrastructure issues that contributed to flakiness but
does not fix the core propagation timing issue.

Changes relevant to flaky tests:
- All tests now use embedded DERP + TLS by default (no public DERP dependency)
- Proper CA certificate trust chains (CreateCertificate now returns CA cert
  separately, installed in container trust stores)
- TestACLTagPropagation and TestACLTagPropagationPortSpecific migrated from
  fragile `sleep 3 ; apk add` entrypoints to WithPackages/WithWebserver with
  proper readiness waits
- TestACLPolicyPropagationOverTime was missing embedded DERP/TLS entirely, now
  gets both by default

Observed flake rates across recent PRs (#3130, #3143, #3144, #3134, #3145):
- TestACLTagPropagation: 2/5 PRs (subtests remove-tag-revokes-access and
  multiple-tags-partial-removal)
- TestACLTagPropagationPortSpecific: 1/5 PRs
- TestACLPolicyPropagationOverTime: 1/5 PRs
- TestAuthWebFlowLogoutAndReloginNewUser: 1/5 PRs (ping timeout)

All failures match existing patterns (propagation timeouts, CI resource
contention). The infrastructure fixes should reduce the contributing factors
but the core issue — EventuallyWithT timeouts too short for CI runners on
ACL/tag propagation tests — remains open.
Next time we collect statistic, we should look for flaky runs since the previous update 16/03/2026 as there was a lot of underlying improvements.

Thank you for taking the time to report this issue.

To help us investigate and resolve this, we need more information. Please provide the following:

> [!TIP]
> Most issues turn out to be configuration errors rather than bugs. We encourage you to discuss your problem in our [Discord community](https://discord.gg/c84AZQhmpx) **before** opening an issue. The community can often help identify misconfigurations quickly, saving everyone time.

## Required Information

### Environment Details

- **Headscale version**: (run `headscale version`)
- **Tailscale client version**: (run `tailscale version`)
- **Operating System**: (e.g., Ubuntu 24.04, macOS 14, Windows 11)
- **Deployment method**: (binary, Docker, Kubernetes, etc.)
- **Reverse proxy**: (if applicable: nginx, Traefik, Caddy, etc. - include configuration)

### Debug Information

Please follow our [Debugging and Troubleshooting Guide](https://headscale.net/stable/ref/debug/) and provide:

1. **Client netmap dump** (from affected Tailscale client):

   ```bash
   tailscale debug netmap > netmap.json
   ```

2. **Client status dump** (from affected Tailscale client):

   ```bash
   tailscale status --json > status.json
   ```

3. **Tailscale client logs** (if experiencing client issues):

   ```bash
   tailscale debug daemon-logs
   ```

   > [!IMPORTANT]
   > We need logs from **multiple nodes** to understand the full picture:
   >
   > - The node(s) initiating connections
   > - The node(s) being connected to
   >
   > Without logs from both sides, we cannot diagnose connectivity issues.

4. **Headscale server logs** with `log.level: trace` enabled

5. **Headscale configuration** (with sensitive values redacted - see rules below)

6. **ACL/Policy configuration** (if using ACLs)

7. **Proxy/Docker configuration** (if applicable - nginx.conf, docker-compose.yml, Traefik config, etc.)

## Formatting Requirements

- **Attach long files** - Do not paste large logs or configurations inline. Use GitHub file attachments or GitHub Gists.
- **Use proper Markdown** - Format code blocks, logs, and configurations with appropriate syntax highlighting.
- **Structure your response** - Use the headings above to organize your information clearly.

## Redaction Rules

> [!CAUTION]
> **Replace, do not remove.** Removing information makes debugging impossible.

When redacting sensitive information:

- ✅ **Replace consistently** - If you change `alice@company.com` to `user1@example.com`, use `user1@example.com` everywhere (logs, config, policy, etc.)
- ✅ **Use meaningful placeholders** - `user1@example.com`, `bob@example.com`, `my-secret-key` are acceptable
- ❌ **Never remove information** - Gaps in data prevent us from correlating events across logs
- ❌ **Never redact IP addresses** - We need the actual IPs to trace network paths and identify issues

> How do I revert the status from expired to not expired without forcing annoying re-adding of the server? This is very tedious and a terrible solution when dealing with non-tech savvy people

```console
headscale nodes expire -d -i $ID
```

With #3285 zero expirations were fixed to `NULL` but in this case the timestamp is slightly off. I've also found a node with this exact timestamp: `1970-01-01 00:02:03` that is not covered by the fix. Representation in the database: `1970-01-01 01:02:03+01:00`

This is caused by a logout via the tailscale CLI/GUI client. It [sets the expiration to `time.Unix(123, 0)`](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/blob/7d18a06292e81f73c8face9ae503b9c16914ea55/control/controlclient/direct.go#L800-L801).

cases.title: [Feature] DNS - Allow Emitting Routes for Domain Names Outside of base_domain / Arbitrary DNS Records
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

**This issue's original body is framed somewhat inaccurately due to a lack of ability to test upstream Tailscale behavior.** See [this comment for more details](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/issues/3316#issuecomment-4879253307). Headscale appears consistent with Tailscale's behavior, and this is a feature request to allow formally emitting routes for domain names outside of base_domain.

---

### Current Behavior

Setting Extra DNS Records in Headscale that don't correspond to entries under dns.base_domain do not propagate to clients. 

Additionally, attempting to then set a custom dns server in split dns for an affected domain in the extra dns entries will cause the split dns resolver to be overridden by the extra dns entries, passing the extra dns entries through to clients.

### Expected Behavior

I'm not entirely sure *which* case if either is supposed to be valid. I was originally going to file domain support outside of base_domain sub entries as a feature request, but seeing the second part of this issue makes me question if it is supposed to work.

The desired behavior is in some way be able to set extra DNS entries for any domain on A, AAAA records. If it isn't intended to be possible, then split DNS entries shouldn't be able to cause normally filtered extra DNS entries to override the split DNS targets. 

If this is intentional, the current requirement to set supplementary split dns entries for extra dns records that should work isn't documented, nor to what extent one should write in split dns entries. Optimally, one shouldn't need to define split DNS entries for extra DNS records outside of dns.base_domain.

### Steps To Reproduce

Case A:
1. Create Headscale deployment with extra DNS records, at least one under the set dns.base_domain and one not under.
2. Register and connect a node, and test where each record points, if propagated to the node.
3. Note the record(s) under dns.base_domain register, but others don't.

Case B:
1. Use existing configurations from Case A.
2. Create Split DNS entry with a functional DNS server for each previously failed extra DNS record.
3. (Re)start Headscale deployment.
4. Connect the node again and test where each record points.
5. Note that each record now points based on extra DNS entries rather using the configured DNS server(s) in split DNS config

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: OpenSUSE Leap 16.0
- Headscale version: v0.28 (tag, ghcr.io)
- Podman version: 5.4.2
- Podman variant: Rootful
- deployment type: Quadlet
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

## Case A:

**Config DNS Segment:**

```YAML
dns:
  magic_dns: true
  base_domain: tailnet.example.com
  override_local_dns: false
  nameservers:
    global: []
    split: {}
  search_domains: []
  extra_records_path: /etc/headscale/dns_records.json
```

**Extra Records JSON:**

```JSON
[
    {
        "name": "test.tailnet.example.com",
        "type": "A",
        "value": "100.64.13.163"
    },
    {
        "name": "test.example.com",
        "type": "A",
        "value": "100.64.17.94"
    }
]
```

## Case B:

**Modified Config DNS Segment**:

```YAML
dns:
  magic_dns: true
  base_domain: tailnet.example.com
  override_local_dns: false
  nameservers:
    global: []
    split:
      test.example.com:
        - 1.1.1.1
  search_domains: []
  extra_records_path: /etc/headscale/dns_records.json
```

last_comments.body:
Both behaviours here are the documented tailscaled MagicDNS semantics rather than a headscale bug — here's the mechanism.

**Why a record outside `base_domain` doesn't resolve (case 1).** headscale only marks a name as "route this to MagicDNS" for `base_domain` + search domains and for explicitly configured split-DNS nameservers — `ExtraRecords` are passed through verbatim with no matching suffix generated (`hscontrol/types/config.go`: `cfg.ExtraRecords = dns.ExtraRecords`, `cfg.Routes = splitResolvers()`, `cfg.Domains = [BaseDomain]+SearchDomains`). On the client, a static record only resolves if the query is actually routed to the internal resolver, and Tailscale documents exactly this on the `Hosts` field:

> Adding an entry to Hosts merely creates the record. If you want it to resolve, you also need to add appropriate routes to Routes. — `tailscale.com/net/dns/config.go`

With native split-DNS (systemd-resolved / Windows NRPT) the OS only forwards suffixes in `MatchDomains` (= the keys of `Routes`, `net/dns/config.go` `matchDomains()`) to `100.100.100.100`; a name outside every route/suffix goes to the system resolver and the extra record is never consulted.

**Why adding a split-DNS entry makes the static record "win" (case 2).** That split entry creates a `Routes` suffix, so the client now routes the name to the internal resolver — and there `resolveLocal` checks the host table *before* forwarding (`net/dns/resolver/tsdns.go`: `hosts[domain]` is matched at the top, forwarding only happens on the `RCodeRefused` fall-through). So the static record answers instead of your `1.1.1.1` resolver.

One caveat that explains the "odd/inconsistent" feel: on Apple platforms (and whenever Tailscale is set as a *global* resolver) everything is intercepted, so an extra record resolves even without a matching route (`net/dns/manager.go`, the non-split-DNS branch). So the "outside base_domain" case is platform-dependent.

Net: resolving arbitrary names outside `base_domain` would require headscale to emit a matching route/suffix for them, which is a feature rather than a fix.
Yep, cool to see that it is defined, but obtuse behavior. Updated the issue title and body to be more accurate. This issue needs its labels updated accordingly.

cases.title: [Bug] policy check no longer works without headscale running after update to 0.29
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

v0.29.1:
```
WRN no config file found, using defaults
Error: connecting to headscale: connecting to /var/run/headscale/headscale.sock: context deadline exceeded
```

### Expected Behavior

v0.28.0:
```
Policy is valid
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a valid policy file in current directory
2. Execute `podman run --rm -v ./policy.hujson:/etc/headscale/policy.hujson:ro --entrypoint headscale docker.io/headscale/headscale:0.29.1 policy check --file /etc/headscale/policy.hujson`
3. Change 0.29.1 to 0.28.0 and it works

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Docker image
- Headscale version: 0.29.1 (also 0.29.0)
```

### Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

Trace output:
```
DBG Setting timeout timeout=5000
DBG HEADSCALE_CLI_ADDRESS environment is not set, connecting to unix socket. socket=/var/run/headscale/headscale.sock
TRC home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/cmd/headscale/cli/utils.go:171 > connecting via gRPC address=/var/run/headscale/headscale.sock
Error: connecting to headscale: connecting to /var/run/headscale/headscale.sock: context deadline exceeded
```

last_comments.body:
This is a regression in what `policy check` does, not a connectivity issue. In 0.28.0 the command validated the file **offline**, with no server and no database:

```go
// v0.28.0 cmd/headscale/cli/policy.go
_, err = policy.NewPolicyManager(policyBytes, nil, views.Slice[types.NodeView]{})
```

Since 0.29 it instead calls a running headscale over the API (`cmd/headscale/cli/policy.go`, `checkPolicy.RunE` → `withClient(... CheckPolicyWithResponse ...)`), which is the socket/`context deadline exceeded` you hit without a server.

The `--bypass-server-and-access-database-directly` flag added after 0.29.1 doesn't cover this case either: `openBypassDB` (`policy.go:42`) prompts interactively (`[y/n]`, so it aborts under CI/closed stdin) and then needs a full config + an existing database — not an offline file check.

Reproduced with the official images, no server and no DB:

```
$ headscale:0.28.0 policy check --file policy.hujson   → Policy is valid        (exit 0)
$ headscale:0.29.1 policy check --file policy.hujson   → context deadline exceeded (exit 1)
```

A `main` build behaves the same: default → API timeout; `--bypass…` → interactive prompt, then `Fatal config error` without a config/DB.

The 0.28 path — a structural parse via `NewPolicyManager(bytes, nil, <empty nodes>)`, needing neither server nor DB — is what CI use needs. Restoring it as a parse-only path is a small change; I can open a PR for it.

cases.title: [Bug] IPv6-only nodes have intermittent connectivity and registration issues
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

This looks a lot like an issue with the Tailscale client and not headscale, per se, but I wanted to document it just in case someone else runs into it. 
On a headscale node with a variety of clients (iOS, linux, MacOS), nodes with only IPv6 fail to register with consistency. No testing was done with Windows. 
Example: 
Headscale node is dual-stacked with A and AAAA records, client is dual stacked: no issues
Headscale is dual-stacked with A and AAAA records, client is IPv4-only: no issues
Headscale is dual-stacked with A and AAAA records, client is IPv6-only with a NAT64: Failure in ability to register
Headscale is dual-stacked with only AAAA record, client is IPv6-only with a NAT64: Successful in ability to register
If the A record is re-added, the client will degrade over time as noted in the client alerts. 

From doing packet captures it appears that if there is an A record the Tailscale client will continually try to make that work, trending toward preferring IPv4, which is counter to the default selection algorithm defined in RFC6724. Strangely, when the exact same host connects to tailscale with IPv6-only there are no issues even over months and months of time.

cases.title: [Bug] Inverted HTTP metrics skip condition
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

The HTTP metrics collector skips every request whose method is not OPTIONS. As a result, regular requests such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE are not recorded in http_requests_total or http_request_duration_seconds.

Only OPTIONS requests are currently collected.

### Expected Behavior

The collector should skip only OPTIONS requests and collect metrics for all regular HTTP traffic.

This behavior should apply consistently to both the main and Noise routers, ensuring that requests are properly represented in http_requests_total and http_request_duration_seconds.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Start Headscale v0.29.x with the HTTP and metrics listeners enabled:

   ```yaml
   listen_addr: 127.0.0.1:8080
   metrics_listen_addr: 127.0.0.1:9090
   ```

2. Check the current HTTP metrics:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9090/metrics |
     grep -E 'http_requests_total|http_request_duration_seconds'
   ```

3. Send multiple regular requests to the `/apple` endpoint:

   ```bash
   for i in $(seq 1 10); do
     curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/apple >/dev/null
   done
   ```

4. Check the metrics again:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9090/metrics |
     grep -E 'http_requests_total|http_request_duration_seconds'
   ```

5. Observe that the `GET /apple` requests were not recorded.

6. Send an `OPTIONS` request to the same endpoint:

   ```bash
   curl -i -X OPTIONS http://127.0.0.1:8080/apple
   ```

7. Check the metrics again:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9090/metrics |
     grep -E 'http_requests_total|http_request_duration_seconds'
   ```

8. Observe that the `OPTIONS` request was recorded, demonstrating that the skip condition is inverted.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: N/A — server-side issue independent of the operating system
- Headscale version: 0.29.3
- Tailscale version: N/A — reproducible directly against the Headscale HTTP endpoint
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

N/A

I am pretty sure that the issue is that the email coming from OIDC is not stored in the username field, but in the email field, and we do not expose a way to update this, as OIDC is considered source of truth and not editable. I think it would be accurate to say that we do not have a supported path for migrating users from one OIDC domain to another. 

Per now, I think editing the database (at own risk) would be the approach, but it would be crucial to also get the OIDC unique token right too and this is more complicated than just the email. 

This is potentially something we could look at in the next release, but I suspect it would realistically be something to tackle when we revisit OIDC down the line, and still not guaranteed that we will make it editable.

Sorry, I probably wasn't clear enough, as I think this may be more simple then you're thinking. (or I could be wrong. :) )

Basically yes, the `headscale rename` command does just change the username field -- which is fine.  The email field is actually adjusted automatically the next time the OIDC user logs into Headscale with a new email.  So OIDC _is_ the source of truth for the email field.

So by doing a `headscale rename` and forcing the user to re-login (expire their nodes), we have both the username and email updated properly as `headscale user list` confirms.   However the node info (`node list`) doesn't seem to get its "user" field updated -- at least not until a Headscale restart.   The nodes know they are owned by the new user (ie. `node list --user user@new-domain.com` works) but listing node information still has the old user field info.  

Since a restart of Headscale gets everything into sync, I was assuming it's currently just missing updating that node user field in the in-memory map when the user info is updated.  If that makes sense?

cases.title: [Bug] A node never receives its own approved exit routes (Self.ExitNodeOption stays false after approve-routes); 0.29.4 also broke the re-advertise workaround
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

A node that advertises exit routes never receives its own updated self node after the routes are approved with `headscale nodes approve-routes`. On the node, `tailscale status --json` keeps `.Self.ExitNodeOption = false` and `.Self.AllowedIPs` without `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`, `tailscale status` does not print "offers exit node", and `tailscale debug netmap` shows `SelfNode.Hostinfo.RoutableIPs = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]` next to `SelfNode.AllowedIPs = ["100.64.0.1/32", "fd7a:115c:a1e0::1/128"]`. Nothing changes over time: the node only learns its approved routes when it opens a new map session (`systemctl restart tailscaled`, `tailscale down && tailscale up`).

Up to v0.29.3, withdrawing and re-advertising the routes on the node (`tailscale set --advertise-exit-node=false && tailscale set --advertise-exit-node`) made headscale send the node its self node, which was a usable workaround. Since v0.29.4 that no longer has any effect: `Self.ExitNodeOption` stays `false` after the toggle too.

With headscale logging at `trace`, both the gRPC approval and each half of the toggle end in `node change processing started node.id=1 reason="policy change"` followed by `update sent` on the node's stream, and the node's self stays unchanged (full log below).

### Expected Behavior

After `headscale nodes approve-routes`, the approved node receives a map response carrying its updated self node, so `Self.AllowedIPs` contains the approved exit routes and `Self.ExitNodeOption` is `true` on its live map session, without restarting tailscaled. Re-advertising the routes should keep refreshing the node's self as it did on v0.29.3.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. headscale v0.29.4, one user, no policy.
2. On a node (tailscale 1.102.4): `tailscale up --login-server https://<headscale> --auth-key <key> --advertise-exit-node`.
3. `headscale nodes approve-routes --identifier <id> --routes 0.0.0.0/0,::/0`.
4. On the node, wait a minute, then `tailscale status --json | jq .Self.ExitNodeOption` → `false`; `tailscale debug netmap | jq '.SelfNode | {AllowedIPs, Hostinfo: {RoutableIPs: .Hostinfo.RoutableIPs}}'` shows the routes announced but absent from `AllowedIPs`.
5. `tailscale set --advertise-exit-node=false && tailscale set --advertise-exit-node`, wait → still `false` (on v0.29.3 this step flips it to `true`).
6. `systemctl restart tailscaled` → `true`.

### Environment

- OS: Debian 13 (headscale container and the tailscale node)
- Headscale version: 0.29.4 (image `headscale/headscale:v0.29.4`); the first part also reproduces on 0.29.3
- Tailscale version: 1.102.4
- Number of nodes: 1 (the exit node itself; no other node needed to observe it)
- Policy: none

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Where it comes from (from the v0.29.4 source)

The mapper only adds the self node to a response when the change's `OriginNode` is the receiving node: `isSelfUpdate := r.OriginNode != 0 && r.OriginNode == nodeID` ([`batcher.go:106`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go#L106)), passed as `includeSelf` to `policyChangeResponse` ([`batcher.go:128`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go#L128), [`mapper.go:353-355`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/mapper/mapper.go#L353-L355)).

1. `State.SetApprovedRoutes` always ends with `if routeChange || !c.IsFull() { c = change.PolicyChange() }` ([`state.go:1053-1055`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L1053-L1055)). `c` is never `IsFull()` there, so the gRPC/CLI approval always fans out a bare `PolicyChange()` with `OriginNode == 0`, and the approved node never gets its self. This part is the same on v0.29.3 and on `main`.
2. Since v0.29.4, `NodeView.HasPolicyChange` also compares `ExitRoutes()` ([`node.go:1233`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/types/node.go#L1233), commit 4411264e, cherry-pick of 905ab92f from #3450, backported in #3467). A node re-advertising its already-approved exit routes therefore makes `PolicyManager.SetNodes` return `true` even when the filter hashes match ([`policy.go:900`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go#L900), the "all hashes match" line in the trace), `updatePolicyManagerNodes` returns `change.PolicyChange()` ([`state.go:2899`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L2899)), and `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` returns it before `buildMapRequestChangeResponse` could produce `change.NodeAdded(id)` with its `OriginNode` ([`state.go:3265-3276`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L3265-L3276)). On v0.29.3 the same request ended in `NodeAdded(id)` and `selfMapResponse`, which is why the toggle used to work.

From the code, peers are not affected: the policy response still sends them the node with its routes. Only the node's own view is stale, and nothing refreshes it while its map session stays up.

#2978 / #2996 fixed the same omission for tags by setting `c.OriginNode = nodeID` in `SetNodeTags` ([`state.go:1018`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L1018)). Doing the same for the change returned by `SetApprovedRoutes`, and for the policy change returned from a node's own map request in `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest`, makes the node receive its self node in both cases; I will open a PR. The open draft #3501 rewrites these lines but still returns a bare `PolicyChange()` for an announced route, so it does not change this behaviour.

cases.title: [Bug] 0.29: ViaRoutesForPeer re-resolves the whole policy for every viewer/peer pair; netmap never delivered to nodes with ~950 peers
cases.body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

After upgrading 0.26.1 → 0.27.1 → 0.28.0 → 0.29.4 (one step at a time), our two HA subnet routers never received a netmap again. We had to roll back to 0.26.1 by restoring the database. The policy uses **no `via` grant, no `grants` at all, and no `autogroup:self`** — only `groups`, `hosts`, `tagOwners` and `acls`.

**Tailnet size**

- 1026 nodes (100–180 online), 685 users, PostgreSQL
- 2 HA subnet routers advertising ~60 routes each. They have **946 peers each**; the average node has 5.9 peers (`/debug/nodestore`)
- Policy: 50 `acls` rules, 341 destinations in total, 54 groups listing 2056 usernames

**Symptoms on 0.29.4**

- headscale CPU: 4–9 cores (0.2–0.6 on 0.26.1, ~1.3 on 0.27.1 and 0.28.0)
- Almost every `/machine/map` request ends with `bytes=0`
- Routers register fine (`machineAuthorized=true`), then never reach `Running`
- Clients log `PollNetMap: ... unexpected EOF` every 60 s (reverse proxy read timeout). With the proxy timeout raised to 3600 s, they log `control: map response long-poll timed out!` every 120 s instead, and the request is queued again
- CLI calls exceed the 5 s deadline (`DeadlineExceeded`); `headscale nodes rename` took ~15 s

**Reproduced in isolation**: a local headscale 0.29.4 on a copy of the database, no reverse proxy, **a single client** registered as the router's user. One core is busy at 100 %, one map was eventually delivered after **96 s** (`bytes=366760 elapsed=96213`), the next request ended with `bytes=0` after 157 s because the client gave up at 120 s.

**On 0.26.1, same data, same router**: the netmap arrives within 1 second of registration, and a 30 s CPU profile shows 1.5 s of CPU in total.

**CPU profile on 0.29.4 (production, 6 s, 26 s of samples)** — 89 % of the time is in:

```
mapper.(*Batcher).worker
 mapper.generateMapResponse
  mapper.(*MapResponseBuilder).buildTailPeers
   types.NodeView.TailNode
    state.(*State).RoutesForPeer
     policy/v2.(*PolicyManager).ViaRoutesForPeer     23.27s  89.36%
      policy/v2.(*Group).Resolve                     23.11s  88.75%
       policy/v2.(*Username).resolve                 21.75s  83.53%
        policy/v2.(*Username).resolveUser            14.40s  55.30%
```

**Goroutine dump at the same time**: 106 goroutines waiting in `mapper.(*Batcher).MapResponseFromChange` (called from `AddNode`), 4 workers computing inside `ViaRoutesForPeer`, 2–3 workers waiting on a mutex in `Batcher.worker`.

**What we think happens (reading v0.29.4)**

Three factors multiply:

1. `buildTailPeers` (`hscontrol/mapper/builder.go`) calls `State.RoutesForPeer` → `ViaRoutesForPeer` for **every peer**, including peers that advertise no route at all (only 3 of our 1026 nodes have routes).
2. `ViaRoutesForPeer` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go`) converts every ACL to grants and resolves the sources and destinations of **all** of them before checking `len(grant.Via) == 0`. With no `via` grant in the policy, the result is always empty, so all that work is discarded. The function comment already says: "Hot callers should memoise by (policy-hash, viewer-id) rather than invoking this per-pair."
3. `aclToGrants` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/types.go`) emits **one grant per destination**, each carrying the full source list. Our 50 ACL rules become 341 grants, so a rule with 67 destinations has its sources resolved 67 times.

Each `Username.resolve` walks all users and then all nodes, with no cache, and a username matching no user also builds a formatted error.

For our policy this gives 17 691 username resolutions per (viewer, peer) pair, i.e. about 30 million comparisons per pair and about 28.6 billion for one map with 946 peers, which matches the ~96 s we measured.

Related: #3346 (same symptoms after 0.28 → 0.29.1, on a ~200 device tailnet).


### Expected Behavior

Netmap generation time on 0.29 should stay in the same order of magnitude as on 0.26 for a policy that does not use `via`.

Possible fixes, from cheapest to most complete:

1. In `ViaRoutesForPeer`, return early when no grant in the policy has a `via` tag (ACL-derived grants never have one). This alone removes the cost for every policy without `via`.
2. In `RoutesForPeer` / `buildTailPeers`, skip the via computation for peers that advertise no subnet or exit route.
3. Resolve grant sources and destinations once per policy change (or memoise per policy hash and viewer), instead of once per (viewer, peer) pair.
4. When converting ACLs with `aclToGrants` for this purpose, keep one grant per rule instead of one per destination.

We are happy to test a patch on a copy of our database.


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Use a tailnet with about 1000 nodes and several hundred users, and a policy made of `acls` rules only, with large groups as sources and many destinations per rule (ours: 50 rules, 341 destinations, 54 groups, 2056 usernames). No `grants`, no `via`.
2. Make sure at least one node can see most of the tailnet as peers (in our case a subnet router reachable by everyone: 946 peers).
3. Run headscale 0.29.4 and connect that node.
4. Watch `/machine/map` for that node: the first map takes about 96 s on an otherwise idle server with a single client, and is never delivered when other clients are connected. CPU stays at one full core per busy worker.

Workaround we are evaluating (computed, not yet fully measured): rewriting the `acls` rules as native `grants` with all destinations in one grant (`"ip": ["*"]`) brings the number of source resolutions per pair from 341 down to 52, and removing usernames that match no user brings username resolutions from 17 691 down to 1 025. The compiled filter (`/debug/filter`) is byte-for-byte identical to the one produced by the original `acls` policy.


### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Kubernetes (GKE), official container image
- Headscale version: 0.29.4 (also went through 0.27.1 and 0.28.0; rolled back to 0.26.1)
- Tailscale version: 1.84.2 and 1.102.5 on the subnet routers (containerboot), 1.80 to 1.102 on clients
- Database: PostgreSQL 17
- Policy mode: database
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

We cannot share the database, the policy or client netmaps as they are: they contain real user and customer names. We can produce an anonymised policy with the same shape and the same counts if that helps, and we can test a patch on a copy of the database.

**Policy shape** (mode `database`)

| Section | Count |
|---|---|
| `acls` rules | 50, all `accept`, none with `proto` |
| destinations | 341 in total (335 with port `*`), mostly `hosts` aliases, 34 tags |
| sources | 55 groups, 16 tags, 7 usernames |
| `groups` | 54, listing 2056 usernames (1585 distinct), 1189 of which match no user |
| `hosts` | 65 |
| `tagOwners` | 22 |
| `grants`, `ssh`, `autoApprovers`, `autogroup:*`, `via` | none |

`headscale policy check` accepts this policy on 0.27.1, 0.28.0 and 0.29.4.

**Headscale configuration** (environment variables, secrets and URLs removed)

```
HEADSCALE_POLICY_MODE=database
HEADSCALE_DATABASE_TYPE=postgres
HEADSCALE_PREFIXES_V4=100.64.0.0/10
HEADSCALE_PREFIXES_V6=fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48
HEADSCALE_DNS_MAGIC_DNS=true
HEADSCALE_DERP_URLS=https://controlplane.tailscale.com/derpmap/default
HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_ENABLED=false
HEADSCALE_LOG_LEVEL=info
oidc: enabled, email_verified_required: false
tuning: defaults (we also tried node_store_batch_size=1000, node_store_batch_timeout=5000ms, batch_change_delay=10s, batcher_workers=4, without restoring service)
```

**Resource usage and timings by version** (same tailnet, same evening, Prometheus)

| | 0.26.1 | 0.27.1 | 0.28.0 | 0.29.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU, average (cores) | 0.33 | 1.24 | 1.37 | 3.52 |
| CPU, max (cores) | 1.03 | 1.33 | 1.41 | 9.47 |
| `headscale_nodestore_peers_calculation_duration_seconds`, average | n/a | 9.4 s | 7.6 s | 13.0 s |
| subnet routers available | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| first netmap for a router with 946 peers | ≤ 1 s | not measured | not measured | never within 120 s |

**Router log on 0.29.4** (Tailscale 1.102.5, `TS_BOOT_TIMEOUT=4m`, reverse proxy timeout raised to 3600 s)

```
19:00:54 control: RegisterReq: got response; nodeKeyExpired=false, machineAuthorized=true; authURL=false
19:00:54 health(warnable=login-state): ok
19:02:54 control: map response long-poll timed out!

```

**Headscale log on 0.29.4** (isolated reproduction, single client)

```

last_comments.body:
Follow-up with measurements. We reproduced the problem offline on a copy of the database and measured each step of the upgrade path with a real client.

**Protocol**: database restored from a dump taken on 0.26.1, one Tailscale 1.102.5 client registered under the subnet router's user, its 60 routes advertised and approved, then the client restarted with its state. The timer stops when the client is `Running` and has received its peers. Same machine for all runs, no reverse proxy, no other client.

**First netmap for a node with 946 peers**

| Version | First netmap | headscale CPU time | Registering a node |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.26.1 | 2.6 s | 0.1 s | 2.4 s |
| 0.27.1 | 10.3–11.3 s | 10–12 s | 20.0 s |
| 0.28.0 | 10.3–15.4 s | 11–16 s | 18.8–24.1 s |
| 0.29.4 | 82.8–86.1 s | 90–92 s | 11.9 s |

On 0.29.4, after a second restart of the client, the netmap was **never delivered within 600 s** (2 runs out of 2), with `map response long-poll timed out!` every 120 s.

**This is not a deadlock or an endless loop.** Goroutine dumps taken every 25 s during the failing case show one worker computing in `resolveUser` / `AppendToIPSet`, and `headscale_mapresponse_generated_total` keeps increasing slowly. The computation is simply too slow, and the work started for a request that the client has already given up on (after 120 s) is not cancelled, so the queue for that node never drains.

**Where the time goes** (CPU profiles)

| Case | Hot path | Share |
|---|---|---|
| 0.29.4, netmap of the router | `generateMapResponse → buildTailPeers → TailNode → RoutesForPeer → ViaRoutesForPeer → Group.Resolve → Username.resolve → resolveUser` | 90 % |
| 0.29.4, registering a node | `snapshotFromNodes → BuildPeerMap` | 59 % |
| 0.28.0, netmap of the router | `snapshotFromNodes → BuildPeerMap` | 77 % |

**Control experiment**: with an allow-all policy on 0.29.4, the same node gets its netmap in 2.8–7.2 s with 1026 peers. The cost comes from resolving the policy, not from the size of the netmap.

**Workarounds measured on 0.29.4** (no code change)

| Change | First netmap | After restart | Peers |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | 86.1 s | fails at 600 s | 946 |
| `tuning` (`node_store_batch_size=1000`, `node_store_batch_timeout=5000ms`, `batch_change_delay=10s`, `batcher_workers=4`) and `node.routes.ha.probe_interval: 0s` | 98.3 s | fails at 600 s | 946 |
| router converted to a tagged node | 88.8 s | not measured | 946 |
| usernames matching no user removed from groups | 43.9 s | 60.9 s | 946 |
| 477 stale nodes deleted (expired, or offline for more than 90 days) | 36.0 s | 44.8 s | 514 |
| `acls` rewritten as native `grants`, one grant per rule (52 instead of 341) | 19.4 s | 14.2 s | 946 |
| `grants` and unmatched usernames removed | 12.7 s | 12.6 s | 946 |
| `grants`, unmatched usernames removed, stale nodes deleted | 9.0 s | 4.6 s, 8.7 s | 514 |

With the last combination and 12 clients restarted together with headscale (2 routers, 10 regular clients): regular clients get their netmap in 7.9–9.4 s, routers in 12.6 s and 12.9 s.

The `grants` rewrite is equivalent: the compiled filter from `/debug/filter` is identical to the one produced by the original `acls` policy, and the router keeps its 946 peers. All variants pass `headscale policy check` on 0.29.4.

**Takeaways**

- Offline, stale and expired nodes still count as peers, so they cost as much as online ones.
- Writing the same rules as `acls` costs about 4 times more than writing them as `grants`, because `aclToGrants` emits one grant per destination and the sources are resolved again for each of them.
- An early return in `ViaRoutesForPeer` when the policy has no `via` grant should bring 0.29 back to the 0.28 numbers for policies like ours.

Correction to the description above: the 96 s figure came from a log line read during an earlier run; with the protocol described here the first netmap takes 82.8–86.1 s.

Possibly related: #3417, #3108, #3501, #3156.

We can run more measurements on this copy of the database, or test a patch, if that is useful.

@kradalby 
- We hit the same thing on 0.29.3/0.29.4: about 450 nodes, SQLite, a file-mode policy with 5 rules, no via, no groups.
- Same hot path, but through AutoGroup.Resolve (we use autogroup:member/autogroup:tagged as sources) rather than Group.Resolve/resolveUser. That shows it isn't specific to groups. Any source alias pays it.
- Profile: 82% of CPU in ViaRoutesForPeer. The host maxed out every weekday, and the write queue backed up.
- Confirming the reporter's workaround: acls → grants, one per rule, took our 16 effective grants down to 5. That's 3.3× on this path, with an identical compiled filter, which we verified across the whole fleet.

cases.title: Handle CORS headers and OPTIONS method for HTTP API
cases.body:
<!-- Headscale is a multinational community across the globe. Our common language is English. Please consider raising the bug report in this language. -->

**Bug description**

When trying to use a browser to generate API requests (like, hypothetically, if you're building a web frontend for headscale), the browser expects to to use CORS to determine if it can talk to the external server. The browser does this by the following:
* Sending a pre-flight `OPTIONS` request, expecting back a 204 response with the CORS headers attached
* Once the response is accepted, sending the real API request with all the data

For this to work, we need two things:
* The server (headscale) to generate CORS headers (and have it be configurable to set the domains appropriately)
* The server to accept `OPTIONS` requests without authorization.

**To Reproduce**
Generate a fetch request from a browser in a separate domain. Such as:

``` javascript
let apiKey = '<my api key>';
let url = 'https://<my headscale domain>/api/v1/machine';

window.fetch(url, {
    method: 'GET',
    headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`
    }}).then((resp) => resp.json()).then(function (data) {console.log(data);}).catch(function (error) {console.log(error);});});
```

If no CORS headers are specified, you get this nice error in the browser console:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/45954722/172862437-f64c47d2-8ae1-46b1-95ab-87123487c74e.png)


If you have the right headers (if you, for example, inject them with a reverse proxy) but the OPTIONS request is blocked by authorization, you get this nice error instead:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/45954722/172862213-d8c060cf-eb58-4a4b-b486-e8dcf5942364.png)

Because the OPTIONS request is returning a 401 unauthorized when it shouldn't.

Both are not ideal. You can *fix* both with a reverse proxy, but you certainly shouldn't have to. The web server (gin?) should return OPTIONS with a 204 and be setting the CORS headers on all requests (and the CORS headers should be configurable).

**Context info**

These problems were fixed externally by routing through a Caddy reverse proxy using these matching settings:

```
@hs-options {
	host hs.<my-domain>
	method OPTIONS
}
@hs-other {
	host hs.<my-domain>
}
handle @hs-options {
	header {
		Access-Control-Allow-Origin https://<my-frontend-subdomain>
		Access-Control-Allow-Headers *
	}
	respond 204
}
handle @hs-other {
	reverse_proxy http://headscale:8080 {
		header_down Access-Control-Allow-Origin https://<my-frontend-subdomain>
		header_down Access-Control-Allow-Headers *
	}
}
```

cases.title: How to use routes? In Android for example.
cases.body:
<!-- Headscale is a multinational community across the globe. Our common language is English. Please consider raising the issue in this language. -->

<!-- If you have a question, please consider using our Discord for asking questions -->

**Issue description**

I think this is third time I am setting up Headscale. Each previous attempts I gave up as I was unable to configure it the same way as with Wireguard directly. I have three networks at home. All three reachable on docker server. 10.0.107.0/24, 10.0.208.0/24 and 192.168.28.0/24. My goal is to reach all three when I connect to Headscale server with any client. Client should be Windows or Android.

**To Reproduce**

I started the server using Docker. Then created namespace and connected two clients to it. One is another linux server, other is my Android phone. For linux server I added "--advertise-routes=192.168.28.0/24,10.0.107.0/24,10.0.208.0/24" parameter to tailscale command. Then I enabled all three routes on Headscale and this seems to work.

But for Android client I just can not find an option to add this routes client side. So when I am connected I for example can not ping 10.0.107.0/24 devices.

Can I add them on Headscale server side?

**Context info**

Headscale version: 0.17.0-alpha2
Android client: 1.30.1
OS: Linux Ubuntu

```
root@docker-server:~# docker exec headscale headscale nodes list
ID | Hostname      | Name          | NodeKey | Namespace | IP addresses                    | Ephemeral | Last seen           | Online  | Expired
1  | Mi 10T Pro    | mi-10t-pro    | [4LfgH] | clients   | 100.64.0.1, fd7a:115c:a1e0::1   | false     | 2022-09-14 10:39:52 | offline | no
2  | web-wg-server | web-wg-server | [goF/h] | clients   | 192.168.28.1, fd7a:115c:a1e0::2 | false     | 2022-09-14 10:01:20 | offline | no
root@docker-server:~# docker exec headscale headscale machines routes list -i 1

```
